actors.label: Sharded cache in the data center

frames.narration: A customer changes their configuration, for example a DNS record. Cloudflare's 2020 post says one data center is chosen to collect all writes, so that a single place can number them in order. Here the change becomes log entry 0025.

Updates flow down a tree. Intermediate nodes copy the log from the root nodes or from each other. Each one checks that a new entry is exactly one higher than the last it has applied, so a lost entry cannot go unnoticed.

Now a request reaches an edge server. Its Quicksilver instance is a proxy, which holds only a cache on disk, not the whole dataset. It looks in its own cache first. A hit ends the story here, and Cloudflare says that happens for the great majority of reads.

This key is missing from the local cache. In Quicksilver v2 the proxy asks a relay, and the relay first tries the cache shard that holds this key's slice of the key space, on one of the other servers in the same data center.

messages.label: is it in the data center cache?

frames.narration: The shard does not have it either, so the relay forwards the request to a replica on a storage node, which holds the full dataset. The proxy states which log index it has reached, so that the answer matches what the proxy would have seen if it held every key.

The replica may be ahead of the proxy. If the key was changed after index 0025, it returns the older version it kept for this purpose, or not found if the key did not exist yet. Otherwise it returns the current value.

Finally the relay publishes the answered miss to the other servers in the data center. Cloudflare found that a key missed on one server is likely to be missed on another soon, so each server adds it to its cache, and the one that owns the key's shard keeps it for longer.
